lesson.title: The Whole-Trail Review Game
lesson.subtitle: Mixed-mode synthesis across all 30 topics of El Puente

hook.title: The Complete Architecture of Spanish in Your Hands
hook.content: In this final capstone lesson of the main trail, we put every major mechanism on stage together: conversion bridges, verb dynasties, ser vs estar, preterite vs imperfect vs present perfect, desde hace, por vs para, saber vs conocer, double object pronouns (se lo), gustar, the conditional, and the subjunctive!

pattern.title: Thinking in Spanish, Not Memorizing
pattern.content: Notice how every sentence you build is assembled from clear logical blocks rather than memorized phrasebook lines.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the polite conditional 'would please / would like' from its infinitive and ending:
Complete the Verb Dynasty Matrix by writing the 1st-person present ('yo') of 'suponer' ('I suppose'):
exercises.row_law: Every member of the -poner dynasty conjugates identically to poner.
exercises.column_law: Column 1 is the infinitive; Column 2 is the 1st-person singular present (-pongo).
exercises.explanation: poner → pongo, proponer → propongo, suponer → supongo!

exercises.prompt: Select every English sentence that matches the meaning of 'Me gustaría visitar Madrid mañana':
exercises.meaning: I would like / I'd love to visit Madrid tomorrow
renderings: I would like to visit Madrid tomorrow
I'd like to visit Madrid tomorrow
traps: You have to visit Madrid today
exercises.target_answer: I would like to visit Madrid tomorrow
exercises.explanation: Me gustaría + infinitive expresses a polite conditional wish ('I would like to...').

exercises.prompt: Which English word-for-word blueprint mirrors Spanish 'Se lo voy a dar a mi madre'?
exercises.german: Se lo voy a dar a mi madre
exercises.natural: I am going to give it to my mother
options: Herself it goes to give my mother
It to her I give to my mother
I am going to give it to my mother
To-her it I-go to to-give to my mother
exercises.target_answer: To-her it I-go to to-give to my mother
exercises.meaning: I am going to give it to my mother (literal Spanish blueprint: To-her it I-go to to-give to my mother)
exercises.explanation: Se ('To-her', replacing le before lo) + lo ('it') + voy a dar ('I-go to to-give') + a mi madre ('to my mother').

exercises.idea: say: 'I know Madrid, I know your brother, and I know where the station is'
cues: I know Madrid (place → conocer) → Conozco Madrid,
I know your brother (person → conocer + personal a!) → conozco a tu hermano
and I know where it is (fact/clause → saber) → y sé dónde está la estación
idea_parts: I know your brother → conozco a tu hermano
and I know where the station is → y sé dónde está la estación
exercises.target_answer: Conozco Madrid, conozco a tu hermano y sé dónde está la estación
exercises.meaning: I know Madrid, I know your brother, and I know where the station is
exercises.explanation: Conozco Madrid (city), conozco a tu hermano (person + a), y sé dónde está la estación (fact clause + estar for location)!

summary.outcome: Integrate all conversion bridges, verb tenses, pronoun systems, and moods across the entire Spanish course.

use_example.german: Conozco Madrid, comprendo perfectamente lo que dices y ojalá tengas tiempo para celebrar.
use_example.english: I know Madrid, I understand perfectly what you say, and I hope you have time to celebrate.

summary.takeaway: You now own the structural engine of Spanish — every new word you hear will snap into this framework.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Explore the 15 Support Branches along the trail to practice travel, tapas, boot verbs, professions, and daily life in depth!

twist.prompt: Assemble: 'I understand perfectly what you want'

confirmar.etymology_derivation: confirmación → confirmar. Strip -ación, attach -ar. One rule turns hundreds of nouns into verbs.

saber.english_meaning: to know (facts, information, how to do something; sé: I know)
saber.context_translation: I know how to speak Spanish.
saber.etymology_derivation: Used for facts, clauses, and skills (sé + bare infinitive, without 'cómo').

conocer.english_meaning: to know, be familiar with (people, places; conozco: I know)
conocer.shift_rule: 1st sg in -zco: conozco (takes personal 'a' before people!)
conocer.context_phrase: Conozco Madrid y conozco a tu hermano.
conocer.context_translation: I know Madrid and I know your brother.
conocer.etymology_derivation: Before a specific person, conhecer ALWAYS requires the personal 'a': conozco a María!

gustar.english_meaning: to be pleasing to (me gusta: I like, lit. it pleases to me)
gustar.shift_rule: Inverted dative experiencer verb (gusta sg. / gustan pl.)
gustar.context_phrase: Me gusta el café y me gustan los libros.
gustar.context_translation: I like coffee and I like books.
gustar.etymology_derivation: Latin gustāre ('to taste') — English gusto and disgust. The thing liked is the grammatical SUBJECT!

gustaría.english_cognate: would please (me gustaría: I would like)
gustaría.english_meaning: would please (conditional: me gustaría = I would like)
gustaría.context_translation: I would like to reserve a table.
gustaría.etymology_derivation: Every Spanish conditional simply glues -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -ían onto the whole infinitive!

ojalá.english_meaning: hopefully, I hope that, if only (always triggers subjunctive!)
ojalá.context_translation: I hope you have a great day!
ojalá.etymology_derivation: Direct Arabic inheritance in Spanish; always triggers the subjunctive mood (tengas, venga, sea)!

poner.english_meaning: to put, to place (pongo: I put)
poner.shift_rule: Root of the -poner family (proponer, suponer, componer)
poner.context_phrase: Pongo el libro en la mesa.
poner.context_translation: I put the book on the table.
poner.etymology_derivation: Latin pōnere — root of propose, suppose, compose, expose.

mantener.context_translation: I want to maintain the tradition.

hecho.english_meaning: done, made (participle of hacer); fact (el hecho)
hecho.shift_rule: Double sound shift: factum → hecho (f→h AND ct→ch!)
hecho.etymology_derivation: Look at Latin factum → Spanish hecho: initial f- became silent h-, AND medial -ct- became -ch-!

se.english_meaning: himself, herself, yourself (usted), themselves; to him/her/them (before lo/la)
se.shift_rule: Reflexive AND the 'se lo' replacement for *le lo
se.context_translation: I tell it to him/her today.
se.etymology_derivation: Whenever le or les meets lo/la/los/las, Spanish softens the tongue-twister *le lo into se lo!

lo.etymology_derivation: Latin illum → lo. Walks one step to the left of conjugated verbs: I it want.

cion.name: The -CIÓN Passport
cion.phonetic_rule: English -tion /-(e)ʃən/ becomes Spanish -ción /-ˈθjon/. Always stressed on the ó, and 100% feminine (la).
cion.historical_linguistics: Descends from Latin third-declension abstract nouns in -tiō (accusative -tiōnem). English borrowed thousands via French; Spanish evolved -ción directly.
cion.philological_note: Because every single -ción noun is feminine, this family hands you grammatical gender for thousands of words without memorization.

dad.name: The -DAD Quality Bridge
dad.phonetic_rule: English abstract nouns in -ty correspond to Spanish -dad /-ˈdað/. 100% feminine (la).
dad.historical_linguistics: From Latin abstract quality nouns in -tās, accusative -tātem. Spanish lenited the intervocalic dental stop to -dad.
dad.philological_note: City (ciudad), reality (realidad), university (universidad). The ending guarantees feminine gender.

mente.name: The -MENTE Adverb Engine
mente.phonetic_rule: Feminine adjective + -mente /-ˈmente/ forms adverbs corresponding to English -ly.
mente.historical_linguistics: Originates from the Latin ablative phrase [adjective] mente ('with a ... mind'). Because mens is feminine in Latin, Spanish preserves the feminine adjective stem.
mente.philological_note: Notice how Spanish preserves the feminine form: exactamente (not exactomente). If the base adjective carries a tilde, it keeps it: fácilmente.

ar_engine.name: The -ar Verb Factory
ar_engine.phonetic_rule: English Latinate nouns in -ation correspond to Spanish first-conjugation infinitives in -ar /-ˈaɾ/.
ar_engine.historical_linguistics: Latin first-conjugation verbs in -āre. English borrowed the noun form; Spanish kept the verb stem alive.
ar_engine.philological_note: The 'celebrar trap': strip the entire -ation before attaching -ar. Celebración → celebrar (not celebratar).

ico.name: The -ICO Bridge
ico.phonetic_rule: English adjectives in -ic / -ical correspond to Spanish -ico /-iko/ (masculine) / -ica (feminine). Always carries a written accent on the antepenultimate syllable.
ico.historical_linguistics: Greek -ikos passed through Latin -icus. In Spanish, these are palabras esdrújulas and must be written with a tilde.
ico.philological_note: Mágico, público, básico, económico, romántico. The tilde tells your voice exactly where to jump.

al.name: The -AL Invariable Passport
al.phonetic_rule: English adjectives ending in -al match Spanish -al /-ˈal/ with identical spelling and gender-invariable singular form.
al.historical_linguistics: Latin adjectival suffix -ālis ('pertaining to'). Both languages kept the spelling; Spanish stresses the final syllable.
al.philological_note: El plan natural, la idea natural: no gender change in the singular.

f_to_h.name: Latin F- ➔ Silent H-
f_to_h.phonetic_rule: Latin initial f- weakened into an aspiration and became completely silent h- in Spanish, while English kept the Latin f- cognate.
f_to_h.historical_linguistics: Castilian contact with Basque/Cantabrian substrate languages lacking initial /f/ caused Latin /f-/ to weaken into silent h-.
f_to_h.philological_note: Hacer ↔ fact/manufacture; hijo ↔ filial; hierro ↔ ferrous; horno ↔ furnace. When you see a silent h-, think f.

ct_to_ch.name: Latin -CT- ➔ Spanish -CH-
ct_to_ch.phonetic_rule: Latin medial -ct- palatalized into Spanish -ch- /-tʃ-, while English kept the learned Latin -ct- form.
ct_to_ch.historical_linguistics: The velar stop /k/ vocalized into a palatal glide [j] which then fused with the dental /t/ into the affricate /tʃ/.
ct_to_ch.philological_note: Noctem ➔ noche (nocturnal); lactem ➔ leche (lactose); factum ➔ hecho (fact); octō ➔ ocho (octave).

pl_cl_fl_to_ll.name: Latin PL-/CL-/FL- ➔ Spanish LL-
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.phonetic_rule: Latin initial consonant clusters pl-, cl-, fl- palatalized into Spanish ll- /ʎ/ (or /ʝ/).
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.historical_linguistics: The initial stop or fricative conditioned progressive palatalization of the liquid /l/ in Western Iberian Vulgar Latin.
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.philological_note: Clāmāre ➔ llamar (claim/clamor); clāvis ➔ llave (clef/clavicle); pluvia ➔ lluvia (pluvial); plēnus ➔ lleno (plenty).
